planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil, ideally tucked among rocks or on a slope that sheds winter wet; this cliff-dwelling species resents soggy, stagnant ground far more than it minds drought.

directions: Oresitrophe is a monotypic Chinese genus closely related to bergenia, native to shaded limestone cliffs and rocky ravines of northern China, where it forms a clump of broad, rounded, coarsely toothed leaves that emerge in spring already tinted bronze-red and color further as the season cools. Unlike evergreen bergenia, it is fully deciduous, sending up airy, branched sprays of small pink-to-white flowers directly from the bare crown before the new leaves unfurl. It is best sited among rocks or on a shaded slope with sharp drainage, since it is considerably less tolerant of wet feet than most woodland perennials, and established clumps resent disturbance. Combine it with hellebores and small ferns in a shaded rock garden where its unusual early bloom and bold foliage texture stand out.

planting.note: Plant rooted stolons or container divisions in spring into constantly moist, humus-rich soil in deep shade, ideally near a stream edge or seep; this species will not tolerate drying out even briefly.

directions: Tanakaea radicans is a monotypic, evergreen, stoloniferous groundcover from the moist forest streambanks of Japan and eastern China, forming a dense low mat of leathery, saw-toothed, strawberry-like leaves that creep outward on wiry runners. In late spring it sends up slender, astilbe-like plumes of small white flowers just above the foliage, adding a brief but welcome froth of bloom to an otherwise deep-shade setting. It needs constant moisture and cool root conditions to thrive, making it best suited to a streamside woodland planting or a shaded, consistently damp spot rather than an average border. Use it as a fine-textured edging groundcover alongside ferns and mosses where soil never dries between waterings.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into permanently moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this subalpine native wants cool, wet roots and struggles wherever summer soil moisture is not reliable.

directions: Leatherleaf saxifrage is a rhizomatous native of subalpine wet meadows, streambanks, and bogs across the Pacific Northwest, Alaska, and the northern Rockies, named for its glossy, leathery, rounded leaves that resemble those of a pyrola. Clusters of small white flowers rise on short stalks in early summer, and the real seasonal draw follows afterward, when the spent flower stems and seed capsules turn a rich brick-red that persists into autumn. It performs best in a cool, consistently wet site such as a bog garden, pond margin, or stream edge rather than an average perennial bed, where drying soil quickly causes the foliage to decline. Pair it with other moisture-loving natives like Darmera or sedges in a naturalistic bog planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into gritty, humus-rich, moist but sharply drained soil tucked among rocks in partial shade; this alpine native dislikes being buried too deep or left in standing water.

directions: Elmera is a monotypic genus endemic to rocky, shaded slopes and cliff ledges of the Olympic and Cascade Mountains of Washington State, closely allied to heuchera and boykinia in general appearance. It forms a small, tidy rosette of rounded, scalloped leaves from which wiry stems carry short racemes of tiny, star-shaped, greenish-yellow flowers in summer. Because it comes from a naturally gritty, well-drained alpine habitat, it is best grown in a shaded rock garden or trough with sharp drainage rather than a rich, heavy border soil, where it is prone to rotting. Its small scale and fine detail make it a specimen plant for close viewing rather than a mass groundcover.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frost danger passes, into moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; in the upper end of its hardiness range it benefits from a sheltered, wind-protected site and winter mulch.

directions: Dichroa febrifuga is an evergreen Asian relative of hydrangea, long used in traditional Chinese medicine (its name literally means 'fever-dispelling') but equally valued as a garden shrub for Gulf Coast and lower-South gardens where true hydrangeas can struggle with heat. It bears loose, lacecap-like clusters of small blue to lavender-blue flowers in late spring through summer, followed by ornamental metallic-blue berries that persist for weeks, both held above glossy, leathery, dark green leaves that remain on the plant through winter in mild climates. It performs best in the dappled shade of taller trees or shrubs with consistently moist, acidic soil, and in colder parts of its range it may be damaged or killed back in hard winters, so treat it as half-hardy north of zone 7. Light pruning after flowering keeps the habit tidy without sacrificing the following season's berries.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained forest-floor soil in full shade; allow it room to spread slowly by rhizomes into an informal colony rather than siting it as a single specimen.

directions: Maple-leaf ainsliaea is a rhizomatous forest-floor perennial native to the beech and deciduous woodlands of Japan, named for its distinctive lobed, maple-like leaves that form a loose, spreading carpet in deep shade. In autumn, well after most woodland perennials have finished, it sends up slender stems topped with small, brush-like white to pale pink composite flowers, giving it a late-season role unusual among shade groundcovers. It spreads gradually by rhizomes into informal drifts under deciduous canopy and asks for little beyond the same cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil favored by hostas and ferns. Because it is slow to establish, give new plantings a season or two before expecting significant spread.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes or container stock in early spring into deep, moist, humus-rich soil in full shade; site it where the emerging shoots will not be damaged by late frost, since new growth can be tender.

directions: Dysosma versipellis is a Chinese woodland relative of our native mayapple, grown chiefly for its large, rounded, umbrella-like leaves that emerge mottled and variably marked before settling into deep green, a leaf habit reflected in its species name versipellis, meaning 'changing skin.' In spring, nodding, dark maroon-red flowers open beneath the leaf canopy near ground level, mostly hidden from view and best appreciated by lifting the foliage, followed later by red berries. Like its relatives it demands deep, consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil and resents being disturbed once established, so choose a permanent shaded site at planting time. Grow it alongside other large-leaved shade perennials such as podophyllum or rodgersia for a bold textural contrast.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; because the species is dioecious, plant both a male and a female specimen if berries are desired.

directions: Helwingia japonica is an East Asian understory shrub grown as a botanical curiosity for its highly unusual flowering habit: tiny greenish flowers are borne not in leaf axils but directly on the upper surface of the leaf midrib itself, a trait shared by only a handful of plants worldwide. The species is dioecious, so male plants produce only small clustered flowers while female plants, once pollinated, develop small black berries seemingly growing out of the leaf surface. Its glossy, deciduous foliage and arching habit make it an interesting textural addition to a shaded woodland border for collectors, though it is grown more for conversation value than for showy bloom. Give it the same cool, moist, humus-rich shade conditions favored by other Asian woodland shrubs, with shelter from drying wind.
